newsitem.title: UK: Britain demands IRA truce for S.Fein talks place.
newsitem.headline: Britain demands IRA truce for S.Fein talks place.

text.p: Britain on Friday challenged the outlawed Irish Republican Army to call an "unequivocal" ceasefire but said IRA weapons must be handed in alongside talks that would then involve its political wing, Sinn Fein.
"What is required for Sinn Fein to join (talks) is an unequivocal restoration of the IRA ceasefire," Britain's Northern Ireland secretary, Sir Patrick Mayhew, said.

It was up to the republicans to prove that any new truce was genuine, he added. "They must establish their commitment to exclusively peaceful methods and show that they abide by the democratic process. Deeds as well as words will be needed. It is for them to find them."
Mayhew was speaking 24 hours after Sinn Fein's chief strategist, Martin McGuinness, set out a shopping list of demands for entry into peace talks.
Britain and Ireland have consistently said they will not countenance Sinn Fein entering peace talks under way in Belfast since June until the IRA renews a shattered 17 month truce.

McGuinness signalled that the IRA would not reinstate a ceasefire which ended in February unless Britain pledged that Sinn Fein would be allowed into talks unconditionally. He added that there must be an end to demands for the IRA to surrender guns as part of the price for Sinn Fein to win a talks seat.

But Mayhew made it clear that Britain was sticking to its demand that the guerrillas give up weapons in tandem with talks, as recommended last January by an independent commission headed by former U.S.senator George Mitchell.

"Martin McGuinness says that decommissioning must, without blocking progress, be dealt with to the satisfaction of all the participants in the process of negotiations," Mayhew said in a speech to business figures.
"We say the way forward is for decommissioning to take place in accordance with the recommendations of the Mitchell Report."
Mayhew's speech was the latest phase of efforts to try to put Northern Ireland's battered peace process on an even keel.

Security chiefs in London and Belfast have warned that the IRA, which is fighting to end British rule over Northern Ireland, might strike at any time in an effort to try to win concessions that would speed Sinn Fein into talks.
